endorsements.title: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for AI-Enabled Device Software Functions (final guidance)
endorsements.quote: Specifically, the public facing document include information about the PCCP as appropriate, including a summary of the plan modification, testing methods, validation activities, and performance requirements to be met in order for modifications to be implemented, and means by which users will be informed of device modifications implemented in accordance with the authorized PCCP.

evidence.title: Regulating Flexibility for Artificial Intelligence FDA Experience with Predetermined Change Control Plans
evidence.outcome: Availability and content of user manuals and labeling for PCCP devices
evidence.effect: User manuals identifiable online for 54% of devices; many lacked performance details or mentioned PCCPs.
evidence.quote: User manuals could be identified online for 54% of devices, though many lacked performance details or mentioned PCCPs.
evidence.sample_unit: FDA-authorized AI/ML-enabled medical devices with PCCPs

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether updating device labeling after AI model modifications keeps users informed of current performance. One descriptive review of 26 FDA-authorized devices with change control plans found user manuals online for 54% of them, and many manuals lacked performance details or any mention of the plan.

perspectives.view: No study compares updated labeling with outdated or absent labeling on any outcome. The single available study is a cross-sectional review of 26 devices that documents the hazard. It shows that labeling gaps exist and does not show that revised labeling closes them. Certainty about the practice's effect cannot be rated from this evidence.

FDA's final guidance on predetermined change control plans says the public-facing document should summarize planned modifications, testing, validation, performance requirements, and how users will be informed. The review of 26 authorized devices suggests that labeling in circulation may not yet reflect this expectation, since manuals were found online for only 54% of devices.

When a model changes and the manual does not, clinicians may calibrate their trust to performance figures that no longer apply. The review found that many manuals omitted performance details altogether, which means users of those devices had no baseline to compare against even before any modification. Whether updated labeling reduces misuse remains untested.

Patients depend on their clinicians knowing how a device performs now. The finding that roughly half of manuals could not be located online suggests that patients and outside reviewers may also lack a way to learn whether a tool changed after authorization.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare user understanding, reliance, and error rates when labeling is updated after a model change versus when it is not. Useful designs would also measure how quickly labeling is revised after a modification and whether clinicians receive and read the notices.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population. The hazard study reviewed device documents and did not report on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users. Readability and language access of updated labeling are therefore unexamined, and administrators serving these populations cannot assume that labeling updates will reach or be understood by their staff and patients.
